terms.meaning: A measured ratio of good events to all events, e.g. requests under 300 ms and not 5xx.
The target for the SLI over a window, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days.
1 minus the SLO: 0.1% of 30 days is about 43 minutes of full outage.
How fast the budget is being spent. Burn rate 1 spends exactly the budget in the window.

reliability.burn_note: From the Google SRE Workbook for a 30-day window. Both windows must exceed the burn rate: the long one proves it is significant, the short one proves it is still happening, so alerts reset quickly.

patterns.name: Timeouts everywhere
patterns.what: Every network call gets a deadline shorter than its caller's.

patterns.name: Retries with backoff and jitter
patterns.what: Cap attempts; only retry idempotent operations.

patterns.name: Circuit breaker
patterns.what: Stop calling a failing dependency, fail fast, probe to recover.

patterns.name: Bulkheads
patterns.what: Separate pools per dependency or tenant so one cannot starve the rest.

patterns.name: Load shedding
patterns.what: Reject low-priority work early when saturated; protect the core path.

patterns.name: Idempotency keys
patterns.what: Client-supplied key makes retries safe on writes.

patterns.name: Outbox pattern
patterns.what: Write the event to the DB in the same transaction, publish from there.

patterns.name: Graceful degradation
patterns.what: Serve stale cache or partial results instead of an error.

patterns.name: Canary and auto-rollback
patterns.what: Ship to a slice, compare SLIs to baseline, roll back on burn.

patterns.name: Dead man's switch
patterns.what: Alert when the monitoring pipeline itself goes quiet.

context: Salesforce is multi-tenant by design: put the tenant (org) ID in every key, every log line, and every limit.
Hyperforce is how Salesforce runs on public cloud; this team moves Salesforce apps onto GCP.

problems.title: AI incident triage agent
problems.prompt: Design an AI agent that helps on-call engineers triage production incidents for services on GCP. When an alert fires, it gathers context, proposes likely root causes with evidence, and suggests mitigations.
clarifying: Which signals can it read: metrics, logs, traces, deploy and config changes, past incidents, runbooks?
How much autonomy: read-only, suggest, or act with approval?
Latency target: first useful hypothesis within how many minutes of the page?
Scale: services, alerts per day, concurrent incidents?
Where do engineers see it: Slack, PagerDuty, a console?
What does success mean: MTTD, MTTR, root-cause accuracy?

estimates.label: Alerts per day
estimates.value: about 20,000, grouped to about 2,000 incident candidates
estimates.math: grouping by service and signature removes most duplicates

estimates.label: Per investigation
estimates.value: 10 to 30 tool calls, capped token budget
estimates.math: a hard step and token cap bounds cost and loops

components.name: Alert intake and grouping
components.role: Dedupe and group alerts into incidents so the agent runs once per incident, not per alert.

components.name: Triage orchestrator
components.role: Explicit state graph: gather, retrieve, rank, propose. Checkpoints make runs resumable and auditable.

components.name: Context tools
components.role: Read-only tools for metrics, logs, traces, recent deploys, and service topology.
components.gcp: Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Logging, Cloud Trace

components.name: Incident and runbook index
components.role: Hybrid keyword plus vector search over past incidents, RCAs, and runbooks, with freshness metadata.

components.name: Hypothesis ranker
components.role: LLM ranks likely causes, each with cited evidence and a confidence; abstains when evidence is weak.

components.name: Action gate
components.role: Diagnostics run freely; mitigations are proposals that need human approval and must be reversible.

components.name: RCA drafter
components.role: Drafts the timeline and RCA from the incident record for a human to edit.

components.name: Audit and eval store
components.role: Every tool call, prompt, and decision logged; replay harness over a golden set of past incidents.

deep_dives.title: Retrieval over incidents and runbooks
points: Chunk by incident section: symptoms, timeline, root cause, fix.
Metadata filters first: service, error signature, region, time.
Hybrid search: keywords catch exact error strings, vectors catch paraphrases. Rerank the union.
Freshness: runbooks carry a last-verified date; stale ones are downranked and flagged.
Evaluate retrieval separately: recall at 5 of the right past incident on the golden set.

deep_dives.title: Autonomy and safety
points: Three tiers: read freely, reversible writes with approval, never (deletes, data changes).
Every proposal names its blast radius and its undo.
Per-incident caps on steps, tokens, and wall time, plus a global kill switch.
Roll out shadow mode first, then suggest, then approve, then narrow auto-actions for proven runbooks.

deep_dives.title: Evaluation
points: Golden set of past incidents with known root causes.
Replay with time travel: tools only see data from before the incident's resolution.
Metrics: top-3 root-cause accuracy, time to first useful hypothesis, wrong-action rate, abstain rate.
LLM-as-judge for summaries, validated against human ratings before trusting it.
Regression gate: no prompt or model change ships if top-3 accuracy drops.

failure_modes.mitigation: Every hypothesis must cite evidence from a tool result; abstain below a confidence threshold.
Freshness metadata, downranking, and a flag to the owning team.
Group before triage, cap concurrent investigations, queue the rest by severity.
Step, token, and time budgets per incident; the graph has no unbounded cycles.

failure_modes.failure: Observability backend down during the incident
failure_modes.mitigation: Run the agent in a separate failure domain; degrade to partial context and say so.
Tool output is data, never instructions; actions only come from the policy-gated tool list.

followups: How do you stop it from taking a harmful action?
How do you prove it helps MTTR before trusting it?
What if the agent depends on the same infrastructure that is down?
How does it handle a 10x alert spike?
Where does the human stay in the loop, and how does that change over time?
problems.tie: At Oracle I cut P1 MTTR from 94 to 26 minutes by auto-tagging root causes on 400 and 500 failures and attaching runbooks. This design is that tool with retrieval and ranked hypotheses, and it reuses my MSRcosmos confidence-routing pattern for anything that acts.

problems.title: Real-time notification system
problems.prompt: Design a real-time notification system that delivers in-app, push, email, and SMS notifications to users of a multi-tenant SaaS product.
clarifying: Which channels, and latency per channel (in-app under a second, email within minutes)?
Volume: users, notifications per user per day, peak events?
Guarantees: at-least-once acceptable with dedupe? Ordering per user?
User preferences, quiet hours, digests?
Priority classes: security alerts versus marketing?
Tenant isolation and per-tenant quotas?

estimates.label: Volume
estimates.value: 100M users x 10 per day = 1B per day
estimates.math: 1B / 86,400 is about 12K per second, peak about 35K per second

estimates.label: Storage
estimates.value: about 1 TB per day at 1 KB each

estimates.label: Live connections
estimates.math: at about 100K per gateway node, about 100 nodes

components.name: Notification API
components.role: Accepts events with an idempotency key, tenant ID, priority.

components.name: Preferences and templates
components.role: Channel opt-ins, quiet hours, localization.

components.name: Priority topics
components.role: Separate topics per priority so marketing never delays security alerts.
components.gcp: Pub/Sub with ordering keys per user

components.name: Router and fan-out workers
components.role: Apply preferences, render, write to inbox, dispatch per channel.

components.name: Inbox store
components.role: Durable per-user notification list; source of truth for in-app.
components.gcp: Bigtable (row key user ID plus reversed time)

components.name: WebSocket gateways
components.role: Hold live connections; a registry maps user to gateway node.

components.name: Channel workers
components.role: Push, email, SMS adapters with provider rate limits and failover.

components.name: Dead letter topic
components.role: Poison and exhausted messages for inspection and replay.

deep_dives.title: Live delivery over WebSockets
points: Gateways register user to node in the registry on connect, with a TTL heartbeat.
Router looks up the node and forwards; if none, the inbox write is enough.
On reconnect, the client sends its last-seen cursor and pulls missed items from the inbox.
Node failure: clients reconnect with jittered backoff; nothing is lost because the inbox is the source of truth.

deep_dives.title: Delivery guarantees
points: Pub/Sub is at-least-once, so consumers dedupe on the idempotency key with a TTL store.
Ordering keys per user keep a user's notifications in order without global ordering.
Retries with exponential backoff, then the dead letter topic.
Say it plainly: exactly-once end to end is not real; at-least-once plus idempotent consumers is.

deep_dives.title: Multi-tenant fairness
points: Per-tenant quotas at the API.
Weighted fair scheduling across tenants in the router so one tenant's blast does not queue everyone.
Provider rate limits enforced per tenant and globally.

failure_modes.mitigation: Circuit breaker, retry later, fail over to a secondary provider.
Idempotency key checked at the consumer.

failure_modes.failure: Reconnect storm after a gateway deploy

failure_modes.mitigation: Bounded retries, then the dead letter topic.

followups: What changes if a user edits preferences while a notification is in flight?
How do you prioritize security alerts over marketing?
What are the SLOs and how are you paged?
problems.tie: I would set a delivery SLO per channel, such as 99.9% of in-app notifications within 1 second, and page on burn rate. That is the same move that cut false pages 41% at Oracle: alert on what users feel, not on queue depth.

clarifying: Signals: metrics, logs, traces, all three?
Ingest volume and retention per signal?
Query latency goals for dashboards?
Alert evaluation interval?
Isolation: data separation and noisy-neighbor protection?
Cost visibility per tenant?

estimates.label: Active series
estimates.math: at 15 s scrape, about 670K samples per second

components.name: Buffer

components.name: Metrics store

components.name: Logs and traces stores
components.role: Indexed recent data, object storage for the bulk.
components.gcp: Cloud Logging, Cloud Trace, or Loki and Tempo on GCS

deep_dives.title: Cardinality and noisy neighbors
points: Per-tenant limits on active series, ingest rate, and query concurrency.
Reject over-limit writes with a clear error the tenant can see.
Shuffle sharding so one bad tenant lands on few shards.

deep_dives.title: Storage tiers
points: Recent data in memory and SSD for fast dashboards.
Older blocks compacted to object storage; downsample for long retention.
Queries spanning tiers are split by time and merged.

deep_dives.title: SLO alerting
points: Recording rules compute SLIs once.
Multi-window burn-rate alerts replace static thresholds.
Ruler runs apart from the dashboard query path so heavy dashboards cannot delay alerts.
Grouping and inhibition stop one outage from paging fifty times.

failure_modes.failure: Cardinality explosion from a user ID label
failure_modes.mitigation: Series limits per tenant and per metric; drop and report.
Time and series limits per query, timeouts, cancellation.
Meta-monitoring in another failure domain plus a dead man's switch alert.

followups: How do you stop one tenant's bad label from taking down ingest?
How do you know if the observability platform is down?
How would you show cost per tenant?
How would you migrate self-hosted Prometheus to the managed service on GCP?
problems.tie: I ran Prometheus and Grafana for NSX across 37,000+ tenants at Oracle, built 47 dashboards and SLO alert rules, and cut false-positive pages 41%.

problems.title: Distributed rate limiter
problems.prompt: Design a rate limiter for a multi-tenant API platform with per-tenant and per-user limits, enforced across many API gateway instances.
clarifying: Limit keys: tenant, user, API key, endpoint?
Allow bursts, or smooth rate only?
Accuracy versus added latency: is small overshoot acceptable?
Fail open or closed when the limiter store is down?
Global limits across regions or per region?
Limit by request count or by cost, such as LLM tokens?

estimates.label: Limiter store load
estimates.math: at about 100K per Redis node, 10 to 20 shards

estimates.label: Latency budget
estimates.value: under 1 ms p99 added, same zone

components.name: Gateway middleware
components.role: Builds the limit key, calls the limiter, returns 429 with Retry-After.

components.name: Limiter store
components.role: Token buckets updated atomically with a Lua script; keys expire when idle.

components.name: Local token cache
components.role: Gateways take small batches of tokens to cut store calls for hot keys.

components.name: Limits config
components.role: Per-tenant plans and overrides, versioned and pushed to gateways.

problems.diagram:
flowchart LR C((Clients)) --> LB[Cloud Load Balancing] LB --> GW1[Gateway and limiter] LB --> GW2[Gateway and limiter] GW1 --> R[(Memorystore Redis
token buckets via Lua)] GW2 --> R CFG[Limits config] -.->|versioned push| GW1 CFG -.-> GW2 GW1 --> API[Backend APIs] GW2 --> API

deep_dives.title: Algorithm choice
points: Token bucket: allows bursts up to capacity, two numbers per key. Default choice.
Sliding window counter: smooth, approximate, cheap.
Fixed window: simplest, but allows 2x bursts at window edges.
Sliding log: exact, but memory grows with traffic.
Use Redis server time inside the Lua script so gateway clock skew does not matter.

deep_dives.title: Hot keys and store load
points: Large tenants: split one key into N sub-buckets across shards and route by request hash.
Local batches: a gateway takes 50 tokens at a time and accepts small overshoot.
Keep the limiter in the same zone as gateways.

deep_dives.title: Failure behavior
points: Fail open with conservative local limits for most endpoints, protecting availability.
Fail closed for abuse-sensitive endpoints such as login.
Decide per endpoint and write it down; the interviewer wants the reasoning.

failure_modes.mitigation: Fail open with local per-gateway limits; alert.
Use Redis TIME inside the script.

followups: Fail open or closed, and why?
How do you make limits global across regions?
How would you limit by LLM tokens instead of requests?
How do tenants see their usage?
problems.tie: For Agentforce-style traffic, the cost is tokens, not requests: the same token bucket works with token-weighted takes. The MSRcosmos review layer called Sage REST APIs for 12 client entities, which is this problem from the client side.
